archetype.name: Game Manager (second-year, still developing)
archetype.definition: A former first overall pick playing a short, low-risk, run-leaning style: he has cleaned up his sacks and bad throws and wins in the 10-19 yard window, but he has not yet earned a vertical passing game.

report.headline: Cleaner pocket, real intermediate touch, but the deep ball still doesn't work.
report.take:
Ward's season line still looks like a struggling young quarterback's: -0.075 EPA per dropback (34th of 47), 5.98 yards per attempt (38th) and a 2.4% touchdown rate that ranks 40th. The comparison that matters, though, is with his own rookie year, and on that measure the progress is real. His bad-throw rate fell from 17.6% to 13.3%, his time to throw dropped from 3.0 seconds to 2.81, and his pressure-to-sack rate fell from 32.2% last season to 19.6%, now 7th-best among 38 charted passers. A year ago he held the ball, took sacks and missed throws. Now he gets it out and keeps the offense on schedule. He has traded some aggressiveness for that, but in his second year it is the right trade.

The passing profile splits sharply by depth. From 10 to 19 air yards he is genuinely good: +0.443 EPA per attempt with a +4.0 CPOE, and that window carries the whole offense. Past 20 yards he is completing 17.4% with two interceptions and -0.658 EPA per attempt, a -21.3 CPOE that says the throws aren't there yet. At the other end, 44 throws behind the line have cost -16.6 EPA, and Tony Pollard's targets alone have cost -16.0. Much of the drag on his efficiency comes from screens and checkdowns to backs that a Robert Saleh offense ranked 26th in pass rate over expected leans on. That reflects the play design and the people around him as much as his accuracy.

The numbers also hide how he plays when the offense opens up. In close fourth quarters he is at +0.319 EPA per play on 46 plays, and the no-huddle has been positive too. Within one score overall he is at -0.148. That gap fits a quarterback who looks better when the script forces the ball into his hands than when he is managing a conservative plan. Third down is the weak spot: 30.6% conversions with an average of 8.3 yards to go, and an air-yards-to-sticks figure of -2.37 that says he often throws short of the marker. Under center has been a turnover problem, with four of his five interceptions on just 36 attempts. That is a small sample, but it points to play-action and drop-back timing he hasn't mastered.

The direction is up. Over the last three games he is at +0.115 EPA per dropback against -0.075 for the season, his sack rate is down to 3.1%, and Week 8 in Cincinnati (304 yards, two touchdowns) was the best game of his career in this dossier. The caveat is that his CPOE over that stretch is -6.5, dragged down by an 11-of-22 game in Indianapolis. The efficiency gain is coming from fewer negative plays and more intermediate shots, not from sharper ball placement.

strengths.title: Owns the intermediate window
strengths.body: His 10-19 yard throws produce +0.443 EPA per attempt with a +4.0 CPOE, and he completes them above expectation. Those dig, out and crosser throws are timing-and-anticipation throws, and they carry his efficiency. Since they come from reads rather than raw arm talent, this should hold.

strengths.title: Sack avoidance has transformed
strengths.body: Pressure turned into a sack 32.2% of the time as a rookie and only 19.6% now, and his sack rate of 5.0% ranks 13th. The faster release (2.81 seconds, down from 3.0) and fewer bad throws suggest real processing growth rather than luck. A line playing a 4th-ranked hit rate helps, but the improvement is mostly his.

strengths.title: Better when the game opens up
strengths.body: In close fourth quarters he is at +0.319 EPA per play with a +5.2 CPOE, far above his overall within-one-score number. On 46 plays that is a hint, not proof. Still, it fits his recent surge in higher-volume, catch-up games like Cincinnati.

concerns.title: No functioning deep game
concerns.body: He is completing 17.4% of throws of 20+ air yards with -0.658 EPA per attempt and a -21.3 CPOE. That is misses, not drops or bad luck on a couple of plays. With 23 attempts it is a modest sample, but his rookie year was similarly short and inaccurate, so expect improvement to be slow. It also caps his touchdown rate, which ranks 40th.

concerns.title: Screens and back targets bleed EPA
concerns.body: Throws behind the line have added up to -16.6 EPA, and Pollard's targets run -0.763 EPA each. This is largely scheme and receiver output on designed short throws, not Ward's decisions. It still counts against his line, though, and it won't change unless the play-calling does.

concerns.title: Third downs end short of sticks
concerns.body: He converts 30.6% of third downs at -0.201 EPA per play, and his air yards to the sticks sit at -2.37. The long average distance (8.3 yards) is partly the run-first offense's fault. Still, too many of his third-down throws stop short of the marker, and that is a real flaw.

trend.note: After bottoming out against Houston (-16.9 EPA), he has posted positive passing EPA in two straight games, capped by a 304-yard game in Cincinnati. His accuracy numbers have not risen with the efficiency, so the climb is real but fragile.

nextGame.headline: Post-bye home date with a top-three defense built against short throws
nextGame.body:
Jacksonville ranks 3rd in defensive EPA, 4th against the pass and 2nd against the run, and its short-pass defense is the best in the league at -0.322 EPA per play. That attacks the underneath half of Ward's game directly. The opening is deep, where the Jaguars rank 29th, but deep is exactly where Ward has been at his worst. With the Jags' offense 3rd in EPA and the run defense stout, a trailing, pass-heavy script is likely, and this defense already draws the 2nd-strongest pass funnel in the league. Expect volume, but tough volume. There is no line posted yet in the dossier.

Availability cuts both ways. Carnell Tate, his most productive target by total EPA, is listed out with a shoulder injury, and his estimated return date is the day of this game, so his status is uncertain. Without him, more falls to Elic Ayomanor (strong per target) and Wan'Dale Robinson (flat). Guard Peter Skoronski and tackle JC Latham both left the Cincinnati game questionable and carry the same return estimate. Losing either would threaten the clean-pocket gains. On Jacksonville's side, safety Eric Murray and DT DaVon Hamilton are out for the season, safety Antonio Johnson was listed out, and Travon Walker is questionable with ribs. A thinned secondary is the best argument that Ward's deep ball could finally connect, and the bye gave him two weeks to prepare.

keyMatchups.title: Underneath throws vs league's best short defense
keyMatchups.body: Jacksonville allows -0.322 EPA on short passes, the stingiest mark in the league, and Ward's under-10 throws are already a net negative. The checkdowns and screens that pad his completion rate should be even less productive here.

keyMatchups.title: Deep shots at a depleted secondary
keyMatchups.body: The Jaguars allow 0.949 EPA on deep throws (29th) and are missing two safeties. Ward's deep CPOE is -21.3, so the opening is there for him to take, not a sure thing. One or two hits would swing his whole line.

keyMatchups.title: Tate's status and the WR pecking order
keyMatchups.body: Tate leads the receivers in total EPA. Jacksonville has held WR1s 4.2 PPR under their averages, yet it allows 0.61 EPA per WR1 target, so the role's numbers are mixed. If Tate sits, Ward's intermediate game leans on Ayomanor.

nextGame.watch: Whether Skoronski and Latham are back and whether Ward attacks Jacksonville's thinned safeties deep, or settles into checkdowns against the league's best short-pass defense.

restOfSeason.body:
The sack-avoidance and bad-throw gains held up for eight games and match a quarterback maturing, so treat them as sustainable. The intermediate efficiency is real too. Expect roughly 180-215 passing yards a game. The offense passes less than situation predicts, but a 24th-ranked defense will keep putting him in catch-up scripts, and those suit him better than his overall line suggests. The touchdown rate should drift up a little from 2.4% toward 0.8-1.3 touchdowns a game as red-zone attempts (six touchdowns already) keep coming. A real jump needs the deep ball to start landing, and nothing in two seasons of data says that's imminent.

The last-three-game EPA surge likely overstates the level, since it arrived with a -6.5 CPOE. Settle on a quarterback hovering near average per dropback rather than clearly above it. His rushing has quietly ticked up from his rookie year and adds a steady floor. The under-center interception spike should calm down, since it rests on 36 attempts.
swingFactors: Health of Skoronski and Latham up front
Carnell Tate's return from the shoulder injury
Any progress on throws of 20+ air yards

confidence.note: Eight starts plus a full rookie season confirm the pocket gains; the deep and under-center splits are small samples.
